When I was a child, I learned to press my ear against the side of a seashell and listen for the ocean. There, in the curve of a broken conch my grandmother kept on her mantle, was the promise that the world could speak to you if you were willing to quiet yourself long enough. The rush that came to me was not really the ocean of course, but air vibrating in the hollow shell, traffic outside, my own pulse. Yet it felt like some whisper from far away, like a door to another room cracked open. That sensation—of presence in absence, of hearing something beyond oneself—has haunted me ever since. It is present when I walk through a city at midnight or wait alone at a rural train station, when I scroll through the endless hallway of the Internet or sit under a canopy of leaves on a humid summer afternoon. The world hums and we, if we pay attention, can hum with it. I want to write about that humming, about noticing, about the shapes that silence takes, about what it means to be alive right now among ruins both ancient and brand-new.

There is a particular stretch of road near my apartment where the city begins to thin. Brick rowhouses with cracked cornices give way to warehouses with busted windows, and then to a chain-link fence behind which a rail yard yawns with lines of rusted cars. At night the sodium lamps throw orange halos onto puddles and cats dart across with stolen fish heads. You can stand on the overpass and look down at the tracks and imagine all the places the rails might lead, their steel lines like sentences running on into distant pages. Trains moan somewhere out of sight. The smell here is of creosote, diesel, and damp earth. It is a place designed for movement but often empty, which makes it perfect for thinking about motion and its inverse, about waiting.

Waiting is one of our most universal and least examined experiences. We wait for the light to change, for our coffee to cool, for a reply to a message, for a test result, for a chapter to end, for children to grow, for grief to soften, for the first snow, for news from someone we've not seen in years. We wait for nothing in particular sometimes, simply filling the hours between tasks with small rituals. The modern world conspires to make waiting feel like a burden, a malfunction in the otherwise smooth machine of productivity. We carry devices that promise immediate communication, instant answers, same-day delivery. Lines are to be avoided. Queues are to be streamlined. Yet there is something strange and luminous about the places we are made to pause. In waiting, we encounter ourselves and others nakedly, without the scaffolding of busyness. In the line at the post office, people turn over their errands in their hands like talismans. At a doctor's office, magazines from months ago are rifled, or eyes drift to a television on mute, reading captions about distant storms.

I once spent a night in an airport in Reykjavik, stranded by a snowstorm that had closed the runways. The cavernous hall was full of bodies draped over chairs, infants crying, someone softly playing a guitar in a corner. For eight hours, we were all in suspension, our itineraries canceled by weather. Plans evaporate in snow. Some people paced and checked the departure boards obsessively, as if watching a kettle might make it boil. Others accepted the interruption and settled into sleep or conversation. I sat against a pillar with my coat balled as a pillow and watched the snow spiral beyond the glass. It was silent, thick flakes falling in a way that softened edges. The hum of the building, the murmur of different languages, became a kind of shared lullaby. It struck me then that waiting, like snow, blankets us all indiscriminately. There is a democracy in being delayed; the CEO and the student, the honeymooners and the laborer, all are grounded by the same storm.

When I am forced to wait in less dramatic circumstances, say in line for a coffee, I try to recall that night. I try to transform the irritation of delay into the curiosity of observation. What are the baristas joking about? What book is the woman in front of me reading while she shuffles forward? Why is the man behind me tapping his foot? This practice of paying attention, of leaning into the small theaters around us, can turn boredom into discovery. My grandmother, the one with the seashell, used to say, "If you sit still, the world will tell you a story." She was a great believer in stories, in taking the long view, in letting things unfurl rather than yanking them out. She grew up in a time before streaming, before push notifications, when the only way to know if your friend across town was home was to walk to their house and knock. That pace, slower and more embodied, cultivated a different muscle in the brain. The muscle of patience is weak in many of us now; we have exercised instead the reflex of immediate gratification. To rebuild that muscle, I have found it helpful to seek out situations where waiting is inevitable, to treat them as opportunities rather than inconveniences.

Once, on a train across the Midwest, I found myself seated next to an elderly man with a hat that said "Korea Veteran." He carried a paper sack with a sandwich and an orange and stared out the window at the endless cornfields. We struck up a conversation that lasted hours. He told me about the winter of 1951, about the sounds artillery makes when it echoes off frozen hills, about love letters folded and unfolded so many times that the paper softened. I shared with him my own trivial stories, and we laughed. That ride, which might have been an exercise in monotony if I had buried my head in a phone, became instead a bridge across decades. The train was delayed two hours due to a freight train ahead of us stalled on the tracks, and that delay, which could have been cause for frustration, was a gift of time to listen. Waiting can be a portal to connection.

It can also be a mirror. In the quiet of a waiting room, anxieties bubble to the surface. Will this test come back positive? Will the mechanic say the repair is too expensive? Will the person we are meeting show up? Our minds, in the absence of distraction, can conjure entire dramas. I have waited for medical results that would alter the course of my life, and in those days, every hour elongated. This is a different kind of waiting, heavy and charged. In those times, we see our own vulnerability. We bargain with fate. We imagine futures. The patience required is not one of convenience but of survival. It is here that we learn that waiting is not passive. It is an act. To wait well is to breathe through uncertainty, to stay present when every instinct clamors to leap ahead or retreat back.

The city around me is itself a palimpsest of waits. The brick factory with boarded windows waits for a developer, for rehabilitation or demolition. The sapling in the cracked sidewalk waits for spring. The people on stoops wait for their partners to come home. The bus shelters hold their clutch of riders, eyes scanning for the headlights of a vehicle that is always "five minutes away." The mural on the wall of the community center shows a parade frozen in time; the faces painted there wait eternally to continue their march. Even the statues of the generals in the park are waiting, perhaps, to be reevaluated by a new generation. Waiting is woven into the city, if you look.

If you step out of the city into the woods, waiting takes on another cadence. Trees wait in rings; they mark time in lines of xylem and phloem. A seed waits in soil for rain. A deer waits at the edge of the clearing for the right moment to emerge. Walking in a forest, you feel the elongated patience of nature. Things operate on scales beyond human urgency. The fallen log is being slowly turned to soil by fungi that do not hurry. The river, even as it rushes, is in a way patient; it will carve the canyon in its own time. There is solace in aligning yourself with these longer waits. It can make the agitation of a late bus seem trivial. To sit on a rock and watch sunlight shift through leaves is to realize that not everything is for immediate consumption.

Yet we have built machines to compress waiting. We have microwave ovens, airplanes, instant messaging. In many ways, this is miraculous. The ability to send a message to someone across the world and receive an answer within seconds would have seemed like magic even a hundred years ago. We avoid waiting because waiting reminds us of limits—of bodies, of time, of not having control. Technology seduces us with the illusion that those limits can be overcome. But even in the most connected, accelerated life, waiting persists. You can order a package and track it in real time, but you still have to wait the thirty hours it takes to travel across a continent. You can summon a car to your door with an app, but you still have to watch the little icon move slowly through traffic.

I am not here to argue for a romantic rejection of modern speed. I like receiving mail promptly. I like being able to talk to my friends instantly. But I am concerned that if we eliminate every pause, if we flatten every wait into convenience, we lose something essential. We lose the chance to let our minds wander, to be bored, to be surprised by the stranger next to us. We lose the skill of sitting with discomfort. We lose the ocean in the seashell because we no longer press it to our ear.

The art of waiting well involves a kind of attention that is both outward and inward. Outward, in noticing the world—how the light shifts across the floor as the day turns, how people's faces change when they think no one is watching, how the mood of a room can be read by the way people hold their shoulders. Inward, in noticing your own reactions—impatience rising, anxious thoughts looping, gratitude surfacing when least expected. These observations make time richer. They fill the interstices with meaning instead of irritation. Sometimes, in the middle of waiting for a late friend, I will catch the exact moment when the afternoon light hits the windowpane in a way that scatters tiny rainbows across the wall. That small gift would have been missed had my friend been on time.

I think about waiting in the context of larger, societal waits. Communities wait for justice, for infrastructure, for recognition. Movements wait for tipping points. There is a political dimension to waiting that is not equitable. Some waits are imposed more heavily on some people than others. A bus rider waits longer in the rain while a car passes. A refugee waits in limbo at a border. A parole hearing is postponed. These waits are not the neutral, meditative spaces of a coffee line; they are charged with power dynamics. To romanticize waiting without acknowledging this would be dishonest. At the same time, the patience and endurance cultivated in these enforced waits can be a source of strength and solidarity. The civil rights movement was full of waits—sit-ins, marches that lasted days, legislative delays. To wait collectively with purpose is different from waiting alone with resignation.

There are also waits that we impose on ourselves, intentionally, as practices. Fasting is a wait between meals that heightens awareness of hunger and of the value of food. Meditation is a wait with ourselves, watching thoughts arise and dissipate like the tide. Artists wait for inspiration, for the right color, for the moment when the work feels finished. Writers wait for the next word, the next sentence, sometimes for years. These waits are not empty; they are charged with potential. They are the breath before the leap. I have experienced writer's block as a kind of waiting room in my mind, sterile and uncomfortable. I have also experienced flow, where waiting drops away because I am fully in the moment. Both states teach different lessons.

In relationships, we wait for texts, for calls, for the words "I love you" or "I'm sorry." We wait for trust to build. We wait for wounds to heal. Sometimes we wait too long, holding onto something that has already passed. Sometimes we don't wait long enough and rush into decisions we regret. Knowing when to wait and when to act is a dance. The pace of another person is not always your pace. Synchronizing requires patience. In love, the waits can be exquisite, the time before a first kiss stretching like taffy. They can also be excruciating, the weeks between seeing someone you long for. Technology again intercedes, offering contact through screens, but physical absence remains. The body knows the difference between a message bubble and a warm hand.

As I write this, I am waiting for the kettle to boil. I am waiting for a friend to arrive to go on a walk. I am waiting for news from a family member about their doctor's appointment. Waiting wraps around these everyday actions like a soft ribbon. The act of writing itself is a way of passing time, of making sense of the spaces between events. We write to bridge waits, to talk to ourselves and to others across time. The words are seashells we press to our ears later, hearing again the rush of a day, the voice of someone who may no longer be with us.

On my desk, next to the shell from my grandmother, there is a small stone with a hole worn through it by the sea. Pebbles like this are considered lucky in some cultures. You can look through the hole and see the world framed differently. Sometimes, when I am impatient, I pick up the stone and peer through. It is a reminder that waits can be apertures, not barriers. They can focus your gaze. The hole was made over years of waves passing, of patience embodied in erosion. It is a teacher.

In the end, waiting is woven into the fabric of existence. We are all waiting for something, even if we don't know it. We are waiting for the next breath, for the next dawn, for the end, whatever it may be. We can choose to fight this, to fill every moment with noise and motion, or we can sometimes surrender, allow the hum of the world to swell in our ears, and see what stories arrive. I think of that shell, of how it taught me that sound can be held in silence, that the ocean is everywhere if you listen. I think of the man on the train and his stories folded like letters. I think of airports full of unexpected companions.

So the next time you find yourself in a queue, in traffic, in the liminal space between what was and what will be, try pressing your ear to the moment as if it were a shell. Listen for the rush beneath the waiting. The world is whispering constantly. In the pause, if you are attentive, you may hear it.

And if all else fails, count the seconds between the click of the turnstile and the arrival of the train, watch how shadows lengthen on the sidewalk, taste the way anticipation makes your tongue dry. Waiting is not nothing. It is a kind of life. It is life.
